items.title: Euro FX futures slide to 16-month lows as dollar finds support.
items.excerpt: Euro FX futures extend their decline for a fourth consecutive session, falling roughly 0.75% to 1.1274 and marking their lowest levels since mid-May 2025. The selloff is primarily driven by sustained strength in the U.S. dollar, which remains near the top of its recent range despite a downward shift across the Treasury yield curve following comments from Federal Reserve officials. Additional pressure on the euro stems from ongoing inflationary and energy-related concerns in the eurozone heading into the winter months. Broad dollar strength is also weighing on other major currencies, with the British pound sliding toward its lows for the year and the Australian dollar facing renewed pressure, while the Japanese yen remains bound within its multi-month range.

items.title: Q4 Outlook for Investors: Raise the bar
items.excerpt: Our Q4 base case is a volatile upward grind, but with much greater dispersion beneath the index. Key points: AI meets expensive money: AI spending can remain strong, but higher funding costs, rapid obsolescence and rising reinvestment needs will increasingly separate companies that can comfortably finance the AI race from those spending simply to stay competitive. items.title: Bonds 101: A simple investor guide to navigating today’s higher yields
items.excerpt: Higher yields have made bonds relevant again, with the right role depending on an investor’s life stage, income needs and tolerance for interest-rate and inflation risk. Key points: Bond yields have risen sharply , making fixed income more relevant again for investors seeking income, diversification or greater portfolio stability. The opportunity is not simply a call that yields have peaked. Higher starting yields mean investors can earn more income while taking a more measured view on interest rates. But higher yields do not necessarily mean it is time to go all-in on long-duration bonds. items.title: Euro futures drop to lowest level since mid-July as dollar gains.
items.excerpt: Euro futures traded lower, reaching 1.1350 before closing near 1.1365, marking the lowest level since mid-July. The decline was driven by U.S. dollar strength following rising inflation expectations and shifting Federal Reserve rate hike expectations. The euro has fallen approximately 3% since its August peak above 1.17. Meanwhile, option-derived volatility increased alongside the market decline, as measured by the CVOL index. Speculators expanded their net short positions last week, extending a continuous net short posture in euro futures since late June.

items.title: British Pound futures bounce as UK consumer confidence hits 2-year high.
items.excerpt: British Pound futures rebounded to close out the week following improved UK consumer confidence and hawkish signals from the Bank of England. After finishing higher in just two of the previous 11 sessions, the pound saw a lift as short covering emerged ahead of the weekend. Support also materialized as UK consumer confidence unexpectedly jumped to a two-year high, with GfK's index rising to minus 13 for September. Market expectations shifted as Bank of England Deputy Governor Sarah Breeden and Governor Andrew Bailey highlighted inflation risks, noting that elevated energy costs could make it increasingly difficult to hold rates steady and leaving further rate hikes on the table.

Attention also shifts to the U.S., where July PCE and August Nonfarm Payrolls will provide the latest view on inflation and hiring ahead of the October FOMC meeting. The CME FedWatch Tool currently reflects a 66.4% probability of another rate hike. Alongside a busy macroeconomic calendar featuring PMIs and inflation figures from across the globe, the earnings schedule offers updates from 18 large-cap companies, including Micron Technology and Nike.

items.title: Has the era of cheap food come to an end?
items.excerpt: From climate shocks, including the effects of El Niño, and rising labour costs to changing welfare standards and technological innovation, food prices may be entering a new structural regime. In this episode, Heidi Richardson and Sreedhar Mahamkali from UBS Research discuss the forces driving this shift, the potential role of technology as a counterbalance, and what a structurally higher food inflation environment could mean for consumers, businesses and markets. *(This information is subject to a disclaimer at the end of this podcast.
